summary:
Caquetá is a department of Colombia and stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Access to facilities and custody are covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

The legal framework does not describe what a visitor meets on the ground in Caquetá. The Guardian reported on 30 July 2024 that armed groups in the department were running a "social cleansing" campaign, with flyers distributed on the street and via WhatsApp naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets. A trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men that she had one week to leave town; she hid for a week and then fled at night. A second trans woman said a friend of hers had been killed. Discrimination in the department confines trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work.

Lethal violence is national in scale. Forty-one trans people were killed in Colombia in 2023, eight between February and April 2024, and thirteen in the first quarter of 2025; the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025. On 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, 32, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia; the assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April, and she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents but no one was arrested, even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Her mother Sandra Borja said: "They killed her for being who she was."

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience.
tangentialFactors:
Targeting in Caquetá is part of a pattern of organised threat campaigns in other Colombian departments. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case, described in reporting as calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict.

The national figures sit against a state that has formally accepted gender persecution. The July 2023 indictments by the Special Jurisdiction for Peace marked the first time the Colombian state acknowledged conflict-driven violence against LGBTI people as a crime against humanity, and the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. Graeme Reid's May 2025 mission warned that widespread discrimination and violence require urgent attention as killings rise, an assessment that applies to Caquetá's flyer campaigns as much as to the cities he visited.

Reported totals differ by source and period: 41 trans people killed in 2023, eight between February and April 2024, thirteen in the first quarter of 2025, and 35 LGBTI murders recorded by the Attorney General's Office between January and May 2025. More than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023 in other reporting.
localsOnly:
Residents change their sex marker by signing a document before a notary, a route available since the rule change approved in June 2015; the examinations by judges that preceded it are no longer the procedure. Identification documents issued nationally carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025.

Residents of Caquetá face an economy that offers trans women few options beyond hairdressing and sex work, a constraint the Guardian documented in July 2024 alongside the threat campaigns. A trans woman who stood as a local election candidate was ordered by three armed men to leave town within a week and left under cover of night after hiding for a week.

Domestic protections run through the 2016 Ministry of Interior decree, which set procedural obligations for government institutions in public education, health care, prisons and for victims of armed conflict, and the May 2018 executive decree of President Juan Manuel Santos extending guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture. Court judgments T-314 of 2011, T-909 of 2011 and T-301 of 2004 oblige public and commercial premises to admit people without discrimination, and a 2011 Constitutional Court ruling protects a trans prisoner's choice of hairstyle and makeup.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Caquetá-specific homicide figure for trans people is sourced; the counts available (41 in 2023, eight from February to April 2024, thirteen in the first quarter of 2025) are national. Whether any arrest has followed the flyer campaigns in Caquetá is unresolved in the sources reviewed.

Whether the notary-based marker change has been applied without obstruction in Florencia and the department's smaller municipalities is not sourced here. The status of the comprehensive trans law under legislative consideration in 2025 is unresolved: no source in this inventory confirms its passage or defeat.

The relationship between the armed groups distributing the "social cleansing" flyers and the signatories of the peace framework is not established by these sources, and no figure for internally displaced trans residents of Caquetá is available.
